absent: Bodies and side effects of generic virtual time helpers, context tracking queries, scheduling primitives, and wakeup core functions.
Numeric values and semantics of task states, poll masks, interrupt offsets, and task flag bits.
Locking, interrupt, and RCU requirements for queue add, remove, and locked wakeup callers.
Behavior of default wake callback, prepare and finish wait helpers, and locked wait functions.
Layout and lifecycle of timer sleeper and high resolution timer helpers beyond their use in timeout waits.
Memory ordering guarantees beyond the paired barrier comment for sleeper visibility.

findings.text: Global and per CPU predicates report whether virtual time accounting is active. Global state follows context tracking while per CPU and current CPU state follow generic helpers. One build configuration always reports inactive on the current CPU.

Task switch accounting notifies the generic layer only when enabled on the current CPU, otherwise it does nothing. Guest enter and exit either delegate to generic guest helpers when enabled or directly mark or unmark the current task as a virtual CPU. A disabled configuration always touches the task mark directly.

Soft and hard interrupt accounting provide paired enter and exit entry points per task. Enter paths charge both virtual time and interrupt time with an interrupt type offset, while exit paths complete virtual time charging and clear the offset for interrupt time. In the routed configuration the interrupt time helper accepts task and offset but performs no action.
Wait queue entry is a record holding a flag word plus an opaque private pointer plus a wake callback plus a doubly linked list node.
Wait queue head is a record holding a spin lock plus a list head anchoring entries. A typedef aliases the head record under a conventional queue head type name.
Exclusive equals 0x01, woken equals 0x02, custom equals 0x04, done equals 0x08, priority equals 0x10. Each value is a single bit mask.
Entry typedef aliases the entry record. Wake callback type is a function pointer taking entry address with wake mode plus flags plus opaque key and returning integer status.

Static and on stack initializers establish empty queues and default entries. Head initialization provides an unlocked spin lock with an empty list, optionally registering a lock class key or reusing on stack storage. Entry initialization clears flags and binds either a task with default wake behavior or a caller supplied callback with null private data.

Activity test reports whether the head list is non empty. Single sleeper test reports whether the list holds exactly one element. Sleeper test issues a full memory barrier paired with the waiter side before reporting activity, ensuring visibility of queue updates.

Insertion places a new entry after any leading priority entries and before the first non priority entry. Exclusive insertion first marks the entry exclusive then uses the same priority aware insertion, while tail variants always append at the end with plain or exclusive marking. Removal unlinks the entry node from its queue.

Wake helpers target normal or interruptible task state with a choice of single, counted, all, locked, or synchronous behavior. Locked forms assume the queue lock is already held, while the synchronous form requests a synchronous wakeup hint.

Poll helpers translate between poll masks and opaque wake keys in both directions. Poll wakeups encode the mask as a key and wake one waiter in normal or interruptible state, with variants for current CPU delivery, locked queue, or synchronous delivery including a locked synchronous form.

Poll free wakeup first checks activity and may skip taking the queue lock for performance. It can therefore race with removal of the last entry while the remover still holds the lock, and safety depends on the remover holding RCU read lock so that freeing is deferred through RCU.

Core wait macro implements prepare, test, sleep, retest, finish. It initializes an exclusive or shared entry, then loops preparing to wait, breaking when condition holds, aborting with signal status when interruptible and pending, otherwise executing a caller sleep command and retesting before finishing. Timeout condition helper preserves remaining time semantics and interruptible helper detects states that allow interruption.

Uninterruptible wait entry points assert sleepable context, take a fast path when condition already holds, then sleep via the core loop using normal scheduling, input output scheduling, caller commands around scheduling, or exclusive queueing.

Interruptible, killable, freezable, idle, and caller state waits share the fast path plus core loop pattern with distinct sleep states and return of signal status. Each offers shared and exclusive queueing forms, and killable adds an input output scheduling form while freezable combines interruptible with freezable.

Timeout forms return remaining time and treat expiry as success when condition becomes true. They combine the core loop with relative jiffy timeouts or monotonic high resolution timeouts with slack, including freezable, interruptible, killable, and idle shared and exclusive variants. High resolution form arms a relative timer unless infinite, aborts with timer expiry status when the sleeper is cleared, then cancels and destroys the on stack timer.

Locked waits loop on a caller supplied wait function while holding the queue lock externally, supporting interruptible shared or exclusive behavior with or without interrupt disabling, then remove the entry and restore running state. Lock with interrupt variant drops the caller spin lock with interrupts enabled around the sleep command and reacquires it after waking.

Queue head spin lock serializes list updates and most wakeups. Locked wake helpers require the caller to already hold that lock. Sleeper visibility relies on a barrier paired with the waiter side rather than always holding the lock, and lock with interrupt waits explicitly release and reacquire a caller lock around scheduling.
Wait header uses an include guard macro to ensure single inclusion.
Public wait wrappers assert sleepable context and evaluate the condition before entering the core loop, returning immediately when already true to avoid needless queueing.

Correctness depends on the double condition test around the sleep command plus balanced prepare and finish pairing. Skipping the retest can miss a wakeup that arrived during sleep setup, and failing to finish can leave a stale entry queued.
